overview:
In Jain cosmology, the expression "two-and-a-half continents" (Aḍhāī-dvīpa) refers to a specific diagrammatic representation of the middle world (madhya-loka), the realm of mortals where human birth and the path to liberation are possible. This middle world is imagined not as a globe but as a series of concentric landmasses and oceans arranged around a central continent called Jambūdvīpa, the "Rose-Apple Continent". The phrase "two-and-a-half continents" does not mean that the universe literally contains only two and a half landmasses; rather, it names a canonical cosmographic scheme that focuses on the portion of the middle world most relevant to human existence and spiritual practice.

In this scheme, Jambūdvīpa occupies the central circle. It is surrounded by a ring of ocean, then another continent, then another ocean, and finally a partial outer landmass that terminates in a chain of mountains and shrines. Because this outermost landmass is not depicted as a complete ring but as an irregular, incomplete band, the entire configuration is traditionally described as "two-and-a-half" continents: Jambūdvīpa as the first, the next full continent as the second, and the incomplete outer landmass as the "half". The oceans between them are equally important, but the conventional name highlights the landmasses where human beings can live and where the Tīrthaṅkaras (ford-makers) appear.

Jain cosmographic paintings and diagrams, known as Aḍhāī-dvīpa paṭas, present this structure in highly stylized form. The landmasses are usually shown in buff or yellow tones, while the oceans appear as blue rings or streamers. At the very center stands Mount Meru (Sumeru), the cosmic axis, rising from Jambūdvīpa. Around it, regions, cities, and sacred sites are carefully mapped according to traditional texts. The outermost mountains and shrines mark the limits of the humanly relevant world-space. These paintings are not merely decorative; they function as visual aids for meditation, teaching, and ritual, reminding viewers of the vastness of the cosmos and the precise location of the human realm within it.

Within the broader Jain cosmological framework, the two-and-a-half continents belong to the middle world (madhya-loka), which itself is only one part of the inhabited universe (loka). Above the middle world lie multiple tiers of heavens (ūrdhva-loka), culminating in the siddha-śilā, the realm of liberated souls. Below it stretch the seven levels of hells (adho-loka), where beings experience the consequences of heavy karmic bondage. The two-and-a-half continents thus form the narrow band in which human birth is possible and where the ethical and spiritual disciplines of Jainism—nonviolence (ahiṃsā), restraint, and meditation—can be practiced with the aim of liberation (mokṣa).

Historically, Aḍhāī-dvīpa diagrams have been produced in manuscript margins, on separate cloth paintings, and as large temple hangings. From at least the fourteenth century onward, Jain communities in western India, especially Gujarat and Rajasthan, commissioned such maps as part of a wider visual culture that includes images of the cosmic man (loka-puruṣa) and the seven hells. Over time, the geometry of the two-and-a-half continents became more formalized: early examples show a relatively soft outer mountain ridge, while later paintings emphasize a strong circular band of mountains, trees, banners, and shrines. Despite stylistic evolution, the underlying cosmological idea remains consistent: the mortal world is a finite, ordered space, carefully measured and mapped, within an eternal, beginningless cosmos.

Theologically and philosophically, the concept of the two-and-a-half continents underscores several key Jain themes. First, it expresses the non-creation of the universe: the cosmos is not made by a god but is an eternal structure described in mathematical and spatial terms. Second, it highlights the rarity and preciousness of human birth, since only in the middle world—and specifically within the regions mapped by the Aḍhāī-dvīpa—can beings follow the path of the Jinas and attain liberation. Third, it integrates ethics with cosmology: understanding where one stands in the universe, and how many realms of existence there are, reinforces the urgency of nonviolence and self-restraint as means to move beyond the cycle of rebirth. For students of Jainism, the two-and-a-half continents are therefore not just an exotic cosmographic curiosity but a central symbol of the Jain vision of reality and the human spiritual journey.

primary_sources.title: Jambūdvīpa-prajñapti (Jambūdvīpa-pannatti)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the Śvetāmbara canonical corpus; specific authorship not individualized
primary_sources.original_text: जम्बूद्वीपं तु मध्ये लोके। ततो समुद्रो द्वीपश्च पुनः।
primary_sources.transliteration: jambūdvīpaṃ tu madhye loke, tato samudro dvīpaś ca punaḥ.
primary_sources.translation: Jambūdvīpa is in the middle of the world. Then there is an ocean and again a continent.
primary_sources.notes: This canonical text describes the structure of the middle world, beginning with Jambūdvīpa at the center and proceeding outward through alternating oceans and continents. While the exact phrase "two-and-a-half continents" (Aḍhāī-dvīpa) is a later technical and visual term, the textual basis for concentric continents and oceans surrounding Jambūdvīpa is found here. The verse cited is representative rather than tied to a single standardized edition, and minor variations in wording occur across manuscripts and recensions.

primary_sources.title: Saṃgrahaṇī-ratna
primary_sources.author: Śrī Dharmasāgara (Śvetāmbara tradition)
primary_sources.translation: In the middle world, starting from Jambūdvīpa, the arrangement of continents and oceans is well known as the "two-and-a-half continents."
primary_sources.notes: Saṃgrahaṇī texts summarize Jain cosmology for teaching and ritual purposes. Later recensions and commentarial traditions explicitly use the term "Aḍhāī-dvīpa" to refer to the mapped sequence of continents and oceans around Jambūdvīpa. The line given here reflects this usage in Sanskritized form; in practice, Prakrit and mixed-language versions also occur. Exact wording varies by edition, and students should consult a critical edition or a qualified teacher for precise textual study.

primary_sources.title: Cosmographic paintings and temple maps (Aḍhāī-dvīpa paṭa tradition)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous Jain artists and patrons in Gujarat and Rajasthan (14th–19th centuries)
primary_sources.notes: Although not a textual source in the strict sense, inscriptions on Jain cosmographic paintings often label the diagram as "Aḍhāī-dvīpa-paṭa". These visual sources are part of the traditional corpus used to teach cosmology. They depict Jambūdvīpa at the center, surrounded by two full continents and an incomplete outer landmass, justifying the name "two-and-a-half continents." The paintings are grounded in canonical descriptions but also reflect regional artistic conventions and may include additional decorative elements not mentioned in the texts.

misconceptions.myth: The phrase "two-and-a-half continents" means that Jainism teaches there are literally only 2.5 landmasses in the entire universe.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain cosmology, "two-and-a-half continents" (Aḍhāī-dvīpa) names a specific concentric arrangement of continents and oceans in the middle world around Jambūdvīpa. It does not claim that the whole universe contains only 2.5 landmasses; rather, it focuses on the humanly relevant portion of the middle world where mortals can live and pursue liberation.

misconceptions.myth: The two-and-a-half continents are purely symbolic and have no connection to detailed cosmological measurement or geography.
misconceptions.reality: While the Aḍhāī-dvīpa diagrams are stylized, they are based on detailed cosmological descriptions in Jain texts that specify distances, sizes, and spatial relationships in mathematical terms. The paintings and maps are didactic representations of a carefully structured cosmos, not arbitrary symbols detached from the textual tradition.

misconceptions.myth: Modern Jain practice no longer pays attention to the two-and-a-half continents, so the concept is only of historical interest.
misconceptions.reality: Aḍhāī-dvīpa maps and related cosmographic images continue to be displayed in temples, homes, and museums, and they are used in teaching, storytelling, and meditation. For many contemporary Jains, these diagrams remain meaningful reminders of the vastness of the cosmos, the centrality of the human realm, and the path to liberation, even if they are not interpreted as literal physical geography in a modern scientific sense.
